I was reading this paper yet again:

**Color Control in Dichromated Gelatin Reflection HologramsBy Stephen P. McGrew**

And this caught my eye and never saw is discussed.

**After removal from the water bath, it is quite easy to observe differential degrees of swelling in areas that have received different levels of exposure.**

Does this mean they just took some micrometers or mircoscope and measure the swelling?

Is he seeing swelling in areas of exposure or is it coloration?

Can it be observed during the bath?

I know this has an effect on color but how much?

The reason why I'm so curious about this is that the only way to tell you have done everything right it seems is when the final hologram is processed. I know Joe said something a while back that really caught my eye, which was the film turned a blue color when fixing (I think) when he got a really bright DCG. If there are intermediary observation points (predictors) along the way, then optimizing quality goes up big time. It means you can cut a problem in half or thirds by observing the condition of the plate during its phases. Or maybe I am smoking something 

Thanks 

Tony

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
My take and understanding on the McGrew statement, "After removal from the water bath, it is quite easy to observe differential degrees of swelling in areas that have received different levels of exposure" is that you should actually be able to see bumps and ridges in your hologram. But not the individual fringes just the areas that received a large overall amount of light. Like if you make a hologram of a coin real close to the plate, after th water swell, you should see and indentation roughly the size of the coin where the coin was. That's my take anyway.

During fixing there is always a blue precipitation out of the emulsion but I really don't recall seeing the plate as blue tinged wheras a weaker hologram was not. Some of the blue precipitate will remain in the gelatin after fixing and prior to washing but again, I did not see a difference. Of course I was not looking for it and will in the future. To me, my opinion only, is a bluer tinted means more unbound CRIII is in the gelatin. Unless of course Joe meant a blue diffraction/reflection color in the fixer and I have not seen or looked for this yet either.

Joe, can you ellaborate on what the blue looked like? TIA

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **Dutchelm05:** The reason why I'm so curious about this is that the only way to tell you have done everything right it seems is when the final hologram is processed.

I would have to agree, Tony. Of course it would be better if there were signposts along the way, but in that respect, I don't think we are very fortunate when it comes to DCG. But you are definitely on the right track with your testing processes. The scientific literature can do as much harm as good, maybe more. The important thing is to trust your own observations, and try to get as good a handle on the variables as possible. Once that is done, I would approach the problem empirically, and not worry about the scientific literature, or even science for that matter. By empirically, I mean just test, observe, make notes, etc. In other words, I would suggest practicing the "craft" of DCG, and borrow those elements of "science" that serve the craft. If it doesn't serve the craft then it's not only useless, but downright harmful.

I can't remember very clearly, but it seems that McGrew was able to note the differences in exposed/hardened DCG versus unexposed/soft simply by running his finger across the emulsion while it was wet. The soft areas would swell to a large extent, while the hard (exposed) areas would resist swelling. I think this was stated in the literature, if not by McGrew, then by someone else. So it was simply a "tactile" observation: the ridges, bumps, or whatever could be felt by running a finger across them.

The "blue" DCG I had mentioned before is rather faint and difficult to notice. It actually seems purple for some reason, and it seems like a very light dyed stain. It should be slightly visible in the hologram I sent you, but it's not present in either of the two you sent me. I have no explanation for it. By the way, the Santa hologram you sent is just as bright (if not brighter) compared to my DCG holograms, for areas of the object that are the same distance from the emulsion. DCG can be tremendously bright for object areas that are nearly touching the emulsion (take for example the ubiquitous coin holograms) but brightness and clarity (for a simple Denisyuk hologram, that is) will rapidly fall off as the object gets deeper.

posts.content_md: Well Tony, once you made a batch of plates, your kind of stuck with them. I believe the most efficient way, as Joe pointed out, is to get your exposure energy and processing down. They take the least time. The mixing, coating and waiting takes the longest. Then since batch to batch AmDi emulsion can change, make your first hologram of something like this [http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/pyracubes6.jpg](http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/pyracubes6.jpg) or an attenuator as you mention. Then you know what is optimal for that batch. Processing is kept standard.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Well, I wouldn't say NO predictor.

Visual inspection of the coating is a great benifit. In fact, I forgot who it was, broght up the technique that you can shine an expanded red laser through a coated and cured plate and see a lot of defomations if there are any like differences in thickness, dirt, etc... I have used this technique and it can help elliminate bad plates in a batch.

Also, inspecting the glare off the emulsion by looking at a glancing angle can prove benificial also.

And inspecting for pits, dust, dirt, etc... helps.

But after the exposure, there is not much you can do.
